meanings.note: Used with para/pra for going back to a place.

examples.text: Vou ter que voltar pra casa da minha mãe.
examples.trans: I am going to have to go back to my mother's house.

meanings.note: Links verbs like faltar to an event or destination.
Assumir a liderança and voltar à liderança are standard election-night phrases for taking the lead.

examples.text: Ela voltou à liderança na pesquisa.
examples.trans: She returned to the lead in the poll.

meanings.note: Used for hot weather: fazer calor (to be hot outside).

examples.text: Eu adoro o calor do verão.
Que calor que tá fazendo aqui!
examples.trans: What heat it is making here!

meanings.note: All-purpose connector, relative link, question opener, and comparative word after mais or melhor.

examples.text: Eu acho que ele já foi.
examples.trans: I think that he already left.

meanings.note: Used here for being present at an event. Vou estar keeps estar in the infinitive after the finite form vou.

examples.trans: I’m not going to be at that meeting.
Are you going to be at that meeting?

meanings.note: Irregular past eu fiz (I made/did); não tem o que fazer means having nothing to do.

examples.text: Ela não tem o que fazer agora.
examples.trans: She has nothing to do now.

examples.text: Esse slide aqui eu fiz ontem.
examples.trans: This slide here I made yesterday.

meanings.note: Points to the speaker's location or reinforces demonstratives like isso aqui and esse slide aqui.

examples.text: Ela veio aqui olhar um extintor.
examples.trans: She came here to check an extinguisher.

meanings.note: Usually contracts with definite articles to no, na, nos, nas.
Expresses duration (por uma hora) and fixed phrases like por exemplo.

examples.trans: I stayed there for an hour.

meanings.note: Used both for love and as an affectionate vocative ('honey, darling').
Links a meeting with its subject. Do is de + the masculine article o; sou do financeiro identifies membership in the finance department.
Subject form referring to the speaker. Explicit eu introduces his department in the explanation.
With que it is Brazil's most natural everyday way to say I think / do you think.

examples.text: Eu acho que você tá exagerando.

meanings.note: Definite article agreeing in gender and number with its noun; also common before given names in casual Brazilian speech.

examples.trans: Look at the young woman over there.

meanings.note: Alone as vocative gente! it means folks/guys; with article a gente it means we/us with third-person singular verbs.

examples.text: Você acha que é melhor que a gente?
examples.trans: Do you think you're better than us?
Oh, folks, the meeting ran late.

meanings.note: Imperfect devia + infinitive is the everyday spoken way to say should (você devia apagar); present deve + infinitive expresses probability (ele deve ter).

examples.text: Ele deve ter sede lá em Orlando.
examples.trans: He must have a branch there in Orlando.

meanings.note: Takes a before an infinitive: começa a fazer (starts doing).

examples.text: A gente começa a fazer a pele.

meanings.note: Used for regularly attending a church, school, or club.

examples.trans: They want to attend a church.

meanings.note: Indefinite article; plural uns and umas mean some or a few in everyday Brazilian Portuguese.

examples.trans: Shall we have a little coffee?

meanings.note: Frequentar uma igreja means to attend a church regularly.

examples.text: A gente devia frequentar uma igreja.

meanings.note: A person being addressed, with third-person verb agreement: você vai, vocês vão. Vai and vão are forms of ir, not forms of the pronoun. Common in Brazil; not a rule that every Brazilian region uses the same address system.

examples.trans: Are you going to the meeting?

meanings.note: Covers knowing facts or finding out information.

examples.text: Eu só quero saber o motivo.
examples.trans: I just want to know the reason.

meanings.note: Used for identifying a type of meeting or the department a person belongs to. The present forms sou and é are irregular.
In um pouco (de), acts as a masculine quantifier noun meaning a little bit.

examples.text: O senhor passou um pouco dos limites.
examples.trans: You crossed the line a little.

meanings.note: Used in Brazil for someone who considers themselves spiritual even without being strictly religious.

examples.text: Ela é uma pessoa muito espiritualizada.
examples.trans: She is a very spiritual person.

meanings.note: A negative answer or a negation in a sentence. A final repeated não can reinforce a conversational refusal in Brazil.
Covers speaking, talking, and telling in everyday Brazilian speech.

examples.text: Deixa eu te falar uma coisa.

examples.trans: They say a lot of things.

meanings.note: Agrees with its noun as a determiner/adjective; singular muita coisa idiomatically means many things.

examples.trans: They say a lot of things.

meanings.note: Neutral demonstrative pronoun pointing to what was just said or done.
Introduces a contrast. The informal thanks softens the refusal; it does not accept the invitation.

examples.trans: It’s a meeting, but I’m not going.

meanings.note: First-person singular object clitic.

examples.trans: Would you help me real quick?

examples.text: Por favor, me deixa morar aqui!

meanings.note: In broadcasts, a você que nos acompanha greets viewers tuning in.

examples.text: Boa noite a você que nos acompanha.
examples.trans: Good evening to you watching us.

meanings.note: Desde que + clause means ever since (desde que eu nasci = since I was born).

examples.text: Moro aqui desde que eu nasci.
examples.trans: I have lived here since I was born.
I have been waiting since early on.

meanings.note: Completed past eu nasci means I was born (active verb in Portuguese, not passive).

examples.text: Moro aqui desde que eu nasci.
examples.trans: I have lived here since I was born.

meanings.note: Informal imperative sente (feel!).
Can mean someone's felt presence or attendance at an event.

examples.text: A presença na reunião é importante.
examples.trans: Attendance at the meeting is important.

meanings.note: In forte aí, colloquial reaction to a wild coincidence.
Reassumir a liderança means to retake the lead once again.
Deixa eu + infinitive is the natural spoken Brazilian frame for let me...

examples.text: Deixa eu te falar uma coisa.

examples.trans: Leave your phone on the desk.

meanings.note: Informal singular object pronoun, routinely mixed with você in warm everyday Brazilian speech.

examples.text: Deixa eu te falar uma coisa.

meanings.note: Vou + infinitive can express a future intention: vou estar means I am going to be. Você takes the third-person vai.
Vamos seguir moves a meeting along to the next topic or slide.

examples.trans: We have to look into it. Let's move on.

meanings.note: One written contraction of em + essa. Feminine singular because reunião is feminine; at is natural English for attendance at a meeting.

examples.trans: I’m not going to be at that meeting.
Are you going to be at that meeting?

meanings.note: Used for a romantic relationship or connection between people.

examples.trans: I am not going to continue in this relationship.

meanings.note: Expresses possession, obligation in ter que + infinitive, and impersonal existence (tem alguns números, there are some numbers).

examples.text: Eu tenho que entrar lá dentro.
examples.trans: I have to go inside there.

meanings.note: Intransitive vamos terminar between partners means let's break up.

examples.trans: It isn't working anymore, let's break up.

meanings.note: Used in na frente de (in front of someone).

examples.text: Não grita na frente dos outros!
examples.trans: Don't shout in front of everyone else!

examples.text: Te espero na frente da sala.
examples.trans: I'll wait for you in front of the room.

meanings.note: Followed directly by an infinitive without a preposition.

examples.text: A gente não conseguiu encaixar direito.
examples.trans: We could not manage to fit it in right.
Did you manage to sort it out?

meanings.note: First-person singular possessive agreeing with the thing possessed.

examples.text: O seu tempo vale mais que o meu?
examples.trans: Is your time worth more than mine?

meanings.note: One's life or daily existence.

examples.text: É isso que você quer pra sua vida?
examples.trans: Is that what you want for your life?

examples.text: A vida no escritório é corrida.

meanings.note: Takes a direct object for payment methods or terms.

examples.trans: Do you all accept a deposit?

meanings.note: Agrees in gender and number; before an adjective (todo travado) means completely.

examples.text: A culpa toda disso foi dele.
examples.trans: All the blame for this was his.
I am all locked up in my neck.

meanings.note: Also appears in todo mundo (everybody).

examples.text: Como bota criança num mundo desse?
examples.trans: How do you bring a child into a world like this?

meanings.note: Introduces a condition; triggers future subjunctive when referring to a possible future action (se vocês olharem).

examples.text: Se eu vou entrar, você vai também.
examples.trans: If I'm going in, you're going too.

examples.text: Se vocês olharem bem, tem números.
examples.trans: If you look closely, there are numbers.

meanings.note: Used enthusiastically in gerund (estou amando) for loving an experience right now.
In até logo it looks ahead to the next meeting. The phrase is added as the lesson farewell, not quoted from the selected source window.
Marks comparisons (mais que), negated continuation (não ... mais, not anymore), and the farewell até mais.
